sections.label: Reading
sections.title: A Training Plan for Northbridge
sections.instructions: Read the passage and answer the questions.
sections.passage:
Northbridge is a fictional design studio with twelve employees. Its managers are considering a system that drafts routine project summaries from approved notes. Currently, staff spend part of each week producing these summaries and checking them with clients. The proposed system may reduce drafting time, but nobody has yet tested how accurately it handles ambiguous notes or unusual requests. The case does not assume that an entire occupation will disappear.

A pilot team proposes a six-week trial. Staff would compare draft summaries with the original notes, record errors and seek client confirmation before anything is finalized. The trial would therefore change the distribution of tasks: less initial drafting might be balanced by more verification, exception handling and communication. Whether the overall workload falls remains an open question.

The studio has only two paid training afternoons available during the pilot. One proposal uses both afternoons to teach system operation. A second divides the time between operation and critical review, including how to identify an unsupported conclusion and explain an uncertainty to a client. The second proposal covers fewer features but may address a wider range of risks.

An employee representative adds that learning outside paid hours would affect workers unequally. Some have caring responsibilities or other commitments. She argues that adaptability should be supported by organizational time and clear procedures, rather than treated solely as an individual personality trait. Managers agree that a certificate alone would not prove competence; employees should demonstrate the skills on realistic examples.

At the end of six weeks, the team plans to review accuracy, total time spent, client corrections and staff feedback. A faster first draft would not count as success if verification or rework increased substantially. The decision to expand the system will depend on the whole process, not on an impressive demonstration.

sections.teacherNotes:
Teacher transcript:
Before we decide which training to buy, I want us to separate two questions. The first is whether staff can operate the new system. The second is whether they can judge its output responsibly. Being able to produce a fluent draft does not establish that the draft is accurate.

I propose using our first training afternoon for basic operation and our second for checking realistic examples. In the review session, people would compare a summary with its source notes, identify unsupported claims and explain unresolved questions to a client. That approach leaves some advanced features for later, which is a real trade-off.

I also want the studio to protect learning time. If employees have to practice after work, those with caring responsibilities may have fewer opportunities. Adaptability should be supported through the way work is organized, not just demanded in a job description.

After six weeks, we should review the time spent on the entire process, including corrections. We should also ask whether employees feel able to challenge an unreliable result. If drafting becomes faster but errors take longer to resolve, we should revise the plan. The goal is a more reliable service and a workforce that can exercise informed judgment, rather than a certificate that everyone receives for attending.

Read the questions aloud for young learners. Replay or reread in short sections if needed.

value.title: A Training Plan for Northbridge
value.purpose: Present an evidence-linked proposal for adapting to workplace change, with prioritized skills, a resource trade-off and a measurable review plan.
value.instructions: Read for the situation, then use evidence to answer.
value.text:
Northbridge is a fictional design studio with twelve employees. Its managers are considering a system that drafts routine project summaries from approved notes. Currently, staff spend part of each week producing these summaries and checking them with clients. The proposed system may reduce drafting time, but nobody has yet tested how accurately it handles ambiguous notes or unusual requests. The case does not assume that an entire occupation will disappear.

A pilot team proposes a six-week trial. Staff would compare draft summaries with the original notes, record errors and seek client confirmation before anything is finalized. The trial would therefore change the distribution of tasks: less initial drafting might be balanced by more verification, exception handling and communication. Whether the overall workload falls remains an open question.

The studio has only two paid training afternoons available during the pilot. One proposal uses both afternoons to teach system operation. A second divides the time between operation and critical review, including how to identify an unsupported conclusion and explain an uncertainty to a client. The second proposal covers fewer features but may address a wider range of risks.

An employee representative adds that learning outside paid hours would affect workers unequally. Some have caring responsibilities or other commitments. She argues that adaptability should be supported by organizational time and clear procedures, rather than treated solely as an individual personality trait. Managers agree that a certificate alone would not prove competence; employees should demonstrate the skills on realistic examples.

At the end of six weeks, the team plans to review accuracy, total time spent, client corrections and staff feedback. A faster first draft would not count as success if verification or rework increased substantially. The decision to expand the system will depend on the whole process, not on an impressive demonstration.

value.title: The Employee Representative’s Proposal
value.purpose: Present an evidence-linked proposal for adapting to workplace change, with prioritized skills, a resource trade-off and a measurable review plan.
value.instructions: Listen once for the situation and again for details.
value.script:
Before we decide which training to buy, I want us to separate two questions. The first is whether staff can operate the new system. The second is whether they can judge its output responsibly. Being able to produce a fluent draft does not establish that the draft is accurate.

I propose using our first training afternoon for basic operation and our second for checking realistic examples. In the review session, people would compare a summary with its source notes, identify unsupported claims and explain unresolved questions to a client. That approach leaves some advanced features for later, which is a real trade-off.

I also want the studio to protect learning time. If employees have to practice after work, those with caring responsibilities may have fewer opportunities. Adaptability should be supported through the way work is organized, not just demanded in a job description.

After six weeks, we should review the time spent on the entire process, including corrections. We should also ask whether employees feel able to challenge an unreliable result. If drafting becomes faster but errors take longer to resolve, we should revise the plan. The goal is a more reliable service and a workforce that can exercise informed judgment, rather than a certificate that everyone receives for attending.
